title: Rain routes: two passages
paragraphs: PASSAGE A — A map after the storm

After several pupils slipped while crossing Meranti School during heavy rain, the environment club began mapping where water remained on the grounds. Members walked the same route twenty minutes after each rainfall, photographed six fixed locations and measured the deepest puddle at each one. They also noted blocked drains and unusually strong wind. Club leader Nara explained that the map was meant to locate recurring trouble, not to prove that every wet surface was equally dangerous.

The first week appeared to confirm the pupils' assumption that the music-room corridor was the main problem. However, leaves had blocked the nearest drain on two of the three survey days. The club cleared it and continued collecting data. The corridor then dried quickly, while shallow water persisted beside the courtyard gate after four different storms. That pattern led the club to move its temporary warning signs from the corridor to the gate.

The school installed a narrow raised strip beside the gate but kept the map active for another month. Early results were encouraging: fewer pupils stepped into the pooled water, although the storms during that month were generally lighter. Nara therefore described the improvement as promising rather than conclusive. The measurements had helped the school make a practical change, but they had not separated the effect of the new strip from the effect of calmer weather.

I was reluctant to wear my cousin's red rain boots. They reached almost to my knees and squeaked against the floor, so I imagined everyone at the community kitchen staring when I arrived to help Aunt Sari deliver evening meals. She ignored my complaints, placed two covered containers in my hands and reminded me that the lane behind the market flooded quickly.

The boots felt clumsy until we reached the third house. There, an elderly neighbour had left her gate open but could not cross the water outside it. I carried the containers through the lane while Aunt Sari held the gate. By the time we returned to the kitchen, mud covered the bright red surface, and the squeak that had embarrassed me had become a useful warning whenever I stepped onto a slippery tile.

Months later, my younger neighbour needed boots for the same delivery route. I almost apologised for the scratches before handing them over, but she grinned at every mark. Watching her disappear into the rain, I understood that the boots had never looked foolish to the people waiting for a meal. The marks I had wanted to hide were evidence that they had travelled where they were needed.
